option_B: The person who greets one while one is working eats pounded yams to his fill; the person who perambulates around the hut employs a pawn; the farmer himself must earn 15,000 cowries before he can eat.
option_C: A diligent worker who drinks from a cracked vessel must eventually seek a new container when the old one finally shatters against the hard farm earth.
option_D: A farmer who secures his drinking vessel poorly will spend his entire day adjusting it instead of enjoying the cool water he worked hard to draw.

proverb: Ilé kì í jó kí oorun kun ojú.
correct_meaning: A house does not burn and fill the eyes with sleep.
original_meaning: A house does not burn and fill the eyes with sleep.
option_A: A family must keep their compound open enough to reveal internal struggles, just as a farmer leaves a harvested gourd visible rather than hiding it away.
option_B: If a wife honors one’s wishes in one’s pres ence and also honors one’s wishes in one’s absence, some reward is certainly due her.
option_C: A dog knows excrement; a pig knows a mud pit; a turkey knows to whom to direct its fart.
option_D: What the climbing rope does to the palm tree, had it done the same to the coconut tree it would have no leaves left.

proverb: Kékeré lọ̀pọ̀lọ́ fi ga ju ilẹ̀ lọ.
correct_meaning: The toad is only slightly taller than the earth.
original_meaning: The toad is only slightly taller than the earth.
option_A: A modest calabash, regardless of the fine beads strung around its neck, will never surpass the height of the soil that bore it.
option_B: A humble calabash, when carefully decorated by the elders, will eventually be elevated to the highest shrine within the compound.
option_C: Only an imbecile says there is no one else like himself; the likes of him are many more than several thousands.
option_D: Were the fox to die, the chicken would not shed a tear; the fox never fostered a chick.

proverb: Kìtì ò mọ́là; ká ṣíṣẹ́ bí ẹrú ò da nǹkan.
correct_meaning: Sudden pouncing does not capture greatness; working like a slave does not ensure anything.
original_meaning: Sudden pouncing does not capture greatness; working like a slave does not ensure anything.
option_A: A poorly carved calabash brings shame to the artisan, proving that hasty labor yields only worthless vessels.
option_B: Just as a smooth calabash slips from the hands, endless toil in servitude fails to secure true prosperity.
option_C: You came to buy yam flour; how did a kid find its way into your calabash?
option_D: The harvest gathered by the humble servant belongs to the compound, reminding us that individual toil feeds the entire lineage.

proverb: Ìdtí ò mátà; woléwolé lẹj bá wí.
correct_meaning: Dirt does not matter; only the sanitary inspector fusses.
original_meaning: Dirt does not matter; only the sanitary inspector fusses.
option_A: Whatever one hands to a warrior to look after is what he looks after.
option_B: Whoever gave the humpback a garment to wear is to blame for his going on an outing from which he will be long in returning.
option_C: The farmer who harvests the crop ignores the soil, while the visiting elder critiques the muddy hands.
option_D: Do not ask me to play the sort of game the gourd played and got a rope around its neck.
